strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical question for NLP-assisted qualitative research: how collaboration settings influence the resulting codebooks. Its focus on human workflows gives the study value beyond comparing automated labeling performance.

Examining three distinct tool families across two contrasting corpora provides useful empirical breadth. Shared initializations within systems improve comparability, and the observed variation across tools, datasets, and evaluation dimensions offers informative descriptive findings.

The evaluation combines consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and manual assignment checks. Evaluating 2,400 document–theme pairs with two annotators and adjudication is a substantial strength; reporting Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.632 and 0.696 makes annotation uncertainty visible.

The manuscript is generally well organized and includes detailed theme inventories, prompt templates, system operations, and a public code/data link. These materials support inspection and potential reuse.
weaknesses: The experimental design does not isolate collaboration modality. Section 4 compares individual codebooks against codebooks produced by three-person synchronous teams; asynchronous consolidation, included in the introduction’s definition, is explicitly omitted. Team size and access to other interpretations therefore change alongside synchrony. Session duration and total human effort are not reported, and returning participants always perform asynchronous work first, introducing possible familiarity effects. The evidence supports exploratory individual-versus-team workflow comparisons, but stronger claims about synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration require additional controls or substantial reframing.

The statistical evidence is insufficiently specified for the central significance claims. Each system–dataset combination has only two synchronous sessions and three asynchronous sessions; consistency consequently has only one synchronous between-codebook comparison. Tables 1–2 report unpaired t-tests without identifying the sampling unit, degrees of freedom, or treatment of participant reuse. Themes and document pairs nested within sessions cannot substitute for independent session replications. Report session-level outcomes, effect uncertainty, and an analysis respecting these dependencies, with appropriate treatment of multiple comparisons. Several significant Climate differences are approximately 0.01, which also warrants more restrained language about their magnitude.

The proposed framework needs stronger validation as a measure of qualitative analysis quality. Maximum-similarity matching permits multiple themes to match the same theme and is sensitive to theme granularity; Table 17 shows substantial differences in theme counts across conditions. SBERT similarity measures semantic proximity, which need not establish equivalent interpretations, especially for opposing stances. Selecting the closest 25% of documents using the same embedding geometry also favors cohesive subsets by construction. Sensitivity analyses controlling theme counts and comparison with human judgments of codebook quality would strengthen claims that higher scores indicate deeper or clearer analysis.

Correctness is not defined sufficiently to reproduce Figure 4. Its vertical axis is labeled F1 score, whereas Section 5.3 describes judging whether sampled document–theme assignments are correct without specifying the prediction targets, precision/recall calculation, or averaging convention. Sampling weights across themes and sessions, evaluation instructions, and uncertainty estimates are also missing. Treatment of unmapped or invalid outputs matters: Table 4 reports invalid-label rates reaching 16.1%. Clarify whether these outputs contribute errors and how coverage affects comparisons.

Participant and session accounting needs reconciliation. The stated design implies 36 synchronous participant slots, but Section 4.2 reports 33 participants and at most one synchronous experiment per participant. Moreover, Tables 15–16 list matching Climate theme inventories for corresponding relational and LLM sessions, leaving codebook reuse unclear. An explicit participant-to-session allocation and account of reused artifacts are necessary to establish experimental independence. The exact SBERT checkpoint and LLM decoding settings should also be specified.

Several explanatory conclusions exceed the available evidence. Two corpora differing simultaneously in domain, size, length, and semantic structure cannot establish that individual dataset characteristics independently drive performance. Likewise, intervention richness varies with the entire system, and one Llama 3.2 3B configuration cannot support broad conclusions about LLM efficiency or reliability. The interviews provide useful observations, but their sample breakdown and analysis procedure are insufficiently described to substantiate general claims about coder experience. These explanations should remain hypotheses. Resolving the design, analysis, and measurement issues through clearer reporting and a narrower exploratory framing is necessary before a sound Findings recommendation.
